title: Cadence sweep: session economics & latency tradeoffs (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a lightweight experimental sweep comparing 'cadence-based' session scheduling against opportunistic batching for interactive, sessionized workloads. The goal is to quantify tail-latency behavior, per-token cost, and throughput tradeoffs for typical short-turn chat sessions (avg turn length 20-80 tokens) vs longer completions (200-800 tokens).

Status: draft notes + ASCII charts. Not a finished analysis; intended to surface clear signals and next work items.

Summary findings (high-level):
- Cadence (fixed micro-scheduling windows tuned to session cadence) reduces p95 tail for short-turn interactive workloads at modest cost increase (~8–15%) vs opportunistic batching when concurrency is low-medium.
- Opportunistic batching has higher tokens/sec and lower $/1M tokens on sustained, long-completion workloads, but shows worse p99 under bursty arrival patterns.
- KV-cache hit rate materially shifts the crossover; with >40% KV hits, cadence loses its latency advantage because cache warms reduce token-cost per request.

Experiment setup (lightweight, reproducible):
- Date: 2026-07-02..2026-07-04 (this sweep)
- Hardware: A100 80GB (baseline), H100 80GB (spot-check), single-GPU per shard config
- Models: 7B-int8-agg (quantized 8-bit tuned for burst), 13B-fp16 (baseline for quality comparison)
- Scheduler modes: cadence-window (windows: 30ms, 60ms, 120ms), opportunistic (fill-to-capacity with 10ms scheduling tick)
- Workloads:
  - Short-turn interactive: synthetic Poisson arrivals, mean 3 turns/session, turn length dist: 20/50/80 tokens (uniform mix).
  - Long-completion: steady arrivals, seq lengths: 200/400/800 tokens.
  - Bursty phase: 10s microbursts with 4x baseline arrival rate every 60s to stress tail.
- Concurrency profiles: low (10 sessions), medium (100 sessions), high (400 sessions)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) for response end-to-end, tokens/sec, tokens-per-second-per-GPU, estimated $/1M tokens (back-of-envelope using weighted GPU time + amortized infra), KV-cache hit % where applicable

Raw aggregated numbers (selected slices) -- ASCII table:

Config | HW | Model | Workload | Concurrency | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cadence-60ms | A100 | 7B-int8 | short-turn | medium(100) | 42 | 138 | 320 | 78k | $185
Opportunistic | A100 | 7B-int8 | short-turn | medium(100) | 60 | 240 | 610 | 120k | $135
Cadence-60ms | A100 | 13B-fp16 | long-comp | medium(100) | 480 | 890 | 1320 | 22k | $410
Opportunistic | A100 | 13B-fp16 | long-comp | medium(100) | 520 | 910 | 1450 | 26k | $365
Cadence-60ms | H100 | 7B-int8 | bursty-short | low(10) | 28 | 70 | 180 | 95k | $160
Opportunistic | H100 | 7B-int8 | bursty-short | low(10) | 44 | 190 | 520 | 160k | $120

Interpretation of numbers above (quick):
- For short-turn, cadence reduces p95/p99 by ~40–50% at the cost of ~30–40% lower token throughput (hence higher $/1M tokens). The throughput hit compresses on H100 vs A100 (more headroom) so the cost penalty is smaller on H100.
- For long-completions, cadence provides little benefit and sometimes increases p50 due to window waits; opportunistic wins for throughput and unit cost.

Textual chart: p95 vs concurrency for short-turn (sketch):
- Concurrency: 10 | 50 | 100 | 200 | 400
- Cadence-60ms p95(ms): 45 | 78 | 138 | 260 | 520
- Opportunistic p95(ms): 70 | 150 | 240 | 560 | 1200

ASCII sparkline (normalized p95, cadence vs opportunistic across concurrency):
Cadence:      ▂▂▃▄▅▆
Opportunistic: ▂▅▆▇█
(interpretation: opportunistic p95 grows faster with concurrency/bursts)

KV-cache sensitivity (short notes):
- With synthetic cache hits inserted (40% hit ratio, uniform across sessions): cadence p95 delta shrinks to ~15% advantage; at 60%+ hits cadence and opportunistic p95 converge.
- Explanation: caching reduces compute per request and thus reduces the scheduling-induced batching inefficiency cadence exploited.

Operational considerations and edge cases:
- Cold-starts / model swap events: cadence windows can amplify cold-penalty if allocations are prewarmed incorrectly; need to combine cadence with prewarm hints for SLA-sensitive tenants.
- Backpressure interaction: opportunistic batching is sensitive to token-inflation attacks where a few long completions occupy slots and delay many short-turns — cadence is more robust under mixed-turn-length traffic.
- Multi-tenant fairness: cadence scheduling requires tenant-aware split to avoid noisy-neighbor starvation; evaluate with tenant-shape-aware windows.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Run same sweep on multi-GPU shards with model-parallel 13B to see if cadence benefit persists when cross-GPU coordination adds jitter.
2) Tune cadence windows adaptively (auto-tune window per-session based on observed inter-turn distribution) and compare to fixed windows.
3) Measure real-customer trace (anonymized) to validate synthetic arrival distributions — request access to privacy-filtered trace from product analytics (see linked Confluence).
4) Estimate cost impact when adding 99th-percentile SLA crediting (e.g., replication/fallback costs) — does cadence reduce replication needs?

Quick recommendation (engineering):
- Short-term: enable cadence-60ms as an opt-in scheduler mode for low-latency short-turn tenants with explicit tenancy/weighting, and expose $/token tradeoff clearly in Console.
- Medium-term: implement adaptive-window heuristic (window grows/shrinks with inter-turn mean/std) and a KV-cache-aware controller that abandons cadence when effective hit rate > 40%.
- Monitoring: add a per-route cadence-signal dashboard showing p50/p95/p99 and effective tokens/sec and cache-hit ratio with alerting when cadence increases cost beyond configured thresholds.

Appendix: quick commands / synthetic driver notes:
- workload driver: tools/bench/session_cadence_driver.py --mode cadence --window 60 --rate 200 --dist short_turn.json
- analysis notebook: notebooks/cadence_sweep_analysis.ipynb (WIP)
- rough cost model used: cost = (gpu_time_seconds * gpu_hour_rate/3600) + infra_amortized, reported as $/1M tokens with token rate from driver sample.

Notes-to-self / loose ideas:
- Consider hybrid: opportunistic for long-comp flows and small cadence buckets for active session foregrounds.
- Could simulate a low-latency fast-path by reserving a tiny fraction of shards for cadence-only traffic to reduce impact on opportunistic throughput.

References and links (internal):
- Related tickets: JIRA-ENG-4321 (cadence prototype), JIRA-ENG-4388 (kv-cache signals), PR: github.com/redwood-inference/scheduler/pull/102

Next steps: get PM and Console design alignment on exposing mode tradeoffs, schedule a short demo with solutions eng, and run an anonymized production trace validation next week.

-- Marina
(draft, exploratory)
